sections.html:
The mansion tax is a 1 percent charge on the sale of a New York residence when the consideration for the whole conveyance reaches $1 million. It comes on top of the regular state transfer tax and is written into Tax Law section 1402-a.

The 1 percent applies to the consideration, or the part of it that belongs to the residential property. Once a sale crosses the line, the tax is figured on the full residential amount, not only on the dollars above $1 million.

The tax is normally the buyer's bill, yet the seller can end up answerable for it. Understand that before signing a contract on any home priced near seven figures.

The buyer pays. Section 1402-a(b) puts the duty on the grantee, and the Department of Taxation and Finance repeats that on its real estate transfer tax page.

If the buyer fails to pay, or is exempt, the duty shifts to the seller. The liability is then joint and several, so the state may collect the whole amount from either party.

The other taxes in a New York sale split differently.

Who pays each New York transfer tax
TaxRate or triggerPaid by
Base transfer tax$2 per $500 of considerationSeller
Mansion tax1% when residential consideration is $1 million or moreBuyer
Additional base tax (New York City only)$1.25 per $500 on residential sales of $3 million or more, or other property at $2 million or moreSeller
Supplemental tax (New York City only)0.25% to 2.9% on residential sales of $2 million or moreBuyer

Residential real property means any premises that is or may be used in whole or in part as a personal residence. The statute names three kinds in particular:

  • a one, two or three-family house;
  • an individual condominium unit;
  • a cooperative apartment unit.

State guidance on the tax adds details that surprise owners. A seasonal cottage that sits empty or is rented part of the year is still residential. So is a house the seller never lived in, as long as it is or may be rented to others as a home.

Building size draws a line. A structure with a store on the ground floor and three apartments above has four units, so it isn't a three-family house. A ten-apartment building doesn't qualify even if the seller lived in one apartment.

The threshold is measured against everything the buyer pays or owes for the property, not only the cash that changes hands. Consideration includes the price, the cancellation of any debt, and the amount of any mortgage or lien, whether the buyer assumes it or takes the property subject to it.

Several rules settle close cases:

  • No lien deduction. The base transfer tax lets a seller of a one to three-family house subtract a continuing lien, but the mansion tax doesn't. An assumed mortgage still counts toward the full price.
  • Seller costs the buyer absorbs count as price. If the buyer agrees to cover the seller's brokerage obligation, that amount is added to the price and can push a sale over the line.
  • Related sellers are added together. Two co-owners who sign separate contracts with one buyer are treated as a single conveyance.
  • Contract assignments are tested separately. When the parties are unrelated and the deal wasn't built to avoid the tax, an assigned contract can be treated as two conveyances, each tested against the line.
  • Mixed use. If a two-family house holds a residential unit and a retail unit, the whole price is tested against the threshold, but tax applies only to the residential portion.

sections.h2: Extra transfer taxes in New York City
sections.html:
New York City sales carry two more state taxes, both added from July 1, 2019. The state's technical memorandum TSB-M-19(1)R explains them.

The additional base tax is $1.25 per $500, paid by the seller. It applies to residential property at $3 million or more, and to other property at $2 million or more. The buyer pays the supplemental tax, which applies to residential sales of $2 million or more at tiered rates on the entire conveyance:

  • $2 million up to $3 million: 0.25%
  • $3 million up to $5 million: 0.5%
  • $5 million up to $10 million: 1.25%
  • $10 million up to $15 million: 2.25%
  • $15 million up to $20 million: 2.5%
  • $20 million up to $25 million: 2.75%
  • $25 million or more: 2.9%

The city also levies its own Real Property Transfer Tax, usually paid as part of closing costs. Ask the title closer for the current city rate on your sale.

sections.h2: When and where the tax is paid
sections.html:
The tax is due no later than the 15th day after the deed is delivered. Tax Law section 1410 sets that deadline, and it also bars a recording officer from recording the deed until the return is filed and the tax is paid.

Outside New York City, the parties file Form TP-584 with the county clerk where the property sits. In the city they file Form TP-584-NYC, and the city's own transfer tax return is built online through ACRIS, the Automated City Register Information System. If a deed won't be recorded, the return and payment go straight to the Tax Department by the same 15-day deadline.

Three filing details can slow a closing. When a limited liability company is the seller or buyer of a building with up to four dwelling units, the filing must include documents naming its members, managers and authorized persons, down to the individuals who own it. Nonresident sellers must compute their gain and pay any estimated income tax due, unless an exemption on the form applies. And both seller and buyer must sign the city's transfer tax return, or the one who didn't sign may face non-filer penalties.

sections.h2: Transfers that avoid the mansion tax
sections.html:
Governmental buyers are exempt, and so are transfers made without consideration. Several nontaxable conveyances matter to families selling a house:

  • A transfer by devise, bequest or inheritance isn't a conveyance at all, so a house passing under a will or by intestacy doesn't trigger the tax at that step.
  • A bona fide gift made without consideration and unconnected to a sale is nontaxable.
  • A transfer given in connection with a tax sale is nontaxable.
  • Conveyances to a nonprofit that holds the land for conservation, parks or historic preservation are exempt from the mansion tax in particular.

A foreclosure or a deed in lieu of foreclosure, by contrast, falls inside the definition of a conveyance. An heir who later sells the inherited house at $1 million or more faces the tax on that sale like any other owner.

sections.h2: Before you sign a contract near $1 million
sections.html:
Read the contract language on who pays which tax first, since the statute sets a default and the contract can shift the base tax. If the buyer agrees to pay the seller's transfer tax, the consideration grows by that amount, and both the base tax and the mansion tax rise with it.

Then ask the closing attorney or title company three questions: does the property fit the residential definition, does any seller concession count as added price, and who will file Form TP-584 and collect the buyer's payment at the table. The seller becomes jointly liable if the buyer doesn't pay, so confirm the filing before the deed is delivered.

faqs.q: Does the New York mansion tax apply to a $999,999 sale?
faqs.a: No, the tax applies only when the consideration for the entire conveyance is $1 million or more. Consideration includes assumed mortgages and obligations the buyer takes over for the seller, so a price just under the line can still cross it once those items are added. Related contracts for the same property are also combined.

faqs.q: Can the seller be forced to pay the mansion tax?
faqs.a: Yes, if the buyer doesn't pay or is exempt. Section 1402-a(b) then puts the duty on the seller, and the liability is joint and several, so the state may collect the full amount from either side. Confirm with the closing attorney that the buyer's payment is made with the return.

faqs.q: Is there a mansion tax on an inherited house?
faqs.a: Not on the transfer to the heir, since a conveyance by devise, bequest or inheritance is outside the definition of a conveyance. The tax can arise when the heir or estate later sells the house for $1 million or more.

faqs.q: What rate does the mansion tax use?
faqs.a: One percent of the consideration, once the consideration for the whole conveyance reaches $1 million. The seller's separate base transfer tax is $2 per $500, and New York City sales add the city and state taxes described above.

faqs.q: Where do I file for the mansion tax?
faqs.a: Outside New York City, file Form TP-584 with the county clerk where the property is located, within 15 days after the deed is delivered. Inside the city, file Form TP-584-NYC, and prepare the city transfer tax packet online in ACRIS. Unrecorded deeds are filed directly with the Tax Department.
